food.text: The Archaic period in North America is taken to last from around 8000 to 1000 BC. It is defined by subsistence economies supported through the exploitation of nuts, seeds, and shellfish. Its end is marked by the adoption of sedentary farming, so the date varies across the Americas.
Around 5000 BC, Native Americans in the Pacific Northwest, from Alaska to California, developed a fishing economy. Salmon was its staple food.

Paleoindians lived alongside and hunted many now extinct megafauna. Most large animals across the Americas became extinct towards the end of the Paleoindian period. The potential role of human hunting in these extinctions has been the subject of much controversy.

Starting around 4000 BC, people across the Southeastern Woodlands exploited wetland resources and created large shell middens. These middens developed where people lived along rivers. There is limited evidence of Archaic peoples along the coastlines before 3000 BC.

Around 7500 BCE, Paleo-Indians began inhabiting the Mesa Verde mesa in increasing numbers. The atlatl, developed during this period, made it easier for them to hunt smaller game. This was a crucial advance at a time when most of the region's big game had disappeared from the landscape.

Starting around 3000 BC, evidence appears of large-scale exploitation of oysters in the Southeast. Archaic coastal sites may have been inundated by rising sea levels. One site in 15 to 20 feet of water off St. Lucie County, Florida, has been dated to 2800 BC.

art.text: Watson Brake in northern Louisiana is an oval of eleven earthwork mounds, three to 25 feet high, connected by ridges. The oval is nearly 900 feet across. Dated to about 3500 BCE, it is considered the oldest earthwork mound complex in North America.

The oldest known art in the Americas may be a fossilized bone, possibly from a mammoth, carved with the profile of a walking mammoth or mastodon. It dates back to 11,000 BCE and was found near Vero Beach, Florida.
art.source_title: Visual arts of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas

art.text: The oldest known painted object in North America is the Cooper Bison Skull, made around 8,050 BCE. It was found in Oklahoma and is painted with a red zig-zag.
art.source_title: Visual arts of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas

art.text: Beginning as far back as 8800 BCE, Paleo-Indians in the American Southwest drilled and shaped multicolored stones and shells into beads and pendants. Jewelry in the Americas has a very ancient history.

The Vero Beach carving was found early in the 21st century in an area where human bones, called Vero man, had turned up in the early 20th century. Those bones were found in association with extinct Pleistocene animals.
art.source_title: Visual arts of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas

art.text: The earliest known examples of North American jewelry are four bone earrings found at the Mead Site, near Fairbanks, Alaska. They date back 12,000 years.
Beads on the Great Plains date back at least to 8800 BCE. That is when a circular, incised lignite bead was left at the Lindenmeier site in Colorado.

The bone carved with a mammoth or mastodon is too mineralized to be dated directly, but the carving has been authenticated as made before the bone mineralized. Its anatomical correctness suggests the artist saw living mammoths or mastodons, more than 10,000 years ago.
art.source_title: Visual arts of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas

art.text: Bone, antler, and possibly marine shell beads from 7000 BCE were found in Russell Cave in Alabama. Olivella shell beads from 6000 BCE turned up in Nevada.
Copper jewelry was being traded from Lake Superior beginning in 3000 BCE, becoming an important material in North American adornment.

war.text: Kennewick Man, whose skeleton washed out of a Columbia River bank near Kennewick, Washington, in 1996, lived about 8,400 to 8,700 years ago. His bones show he had suffered trauma in his lifetime, including a spear jab that healed, and a broken stone projectile point was found embedded in his right ilium, part of the pelvis. Bone had grown around the point, showing that the injury had healed. His skeleton is one of the most complete of such age found in the Americas.

The Old Cordilleran culture lived in the Pacific Northwest from 8000 or 9000 BC until about 3500 BC. Its typical artifact was a simple, leaf-shaped projectile point averaging about 6 cm in length, used as a spear, dart or knife. Hunting mattered most, mainly of deer, bison and other large mammals.
Folsom points served as projectile tips at kill sites, where bison were slaughtered and butchered. Folsom tools were left behind between 9000 BCE and 8000 BCE.
war.source_title: History of Native Americans in the United States

war.text: A projectile found lodged in the hip of Kennewick Man was leaf-shaped, long and broad, with serrated edges. The article describes the point as embedded in his body, but gives no further detail on the wound. It is discussed alongside the Cascade point, a projectile type associated with the Cascade phase, a Native American culture of the Pacific Northwest that existed from 9000 or 10000 BC until about 5500 BC.

Old Cordilleran people originated in Alaska and spread as far as Idaho and the plateaus of California. Their spear points, or points resembling them, have been found as far south as Mexico and South America.

Beyond the healed spear jab, Kennewick Man had a healed fractured rib, a depression fracture on his forehead and a similar indentation on the left side of his head. A broken stone projectile point, about 6 mm thick and made of fine-grained gray volcanic stone, was embedded in his right ilium, part of the pelvis, with bone grown around it, showing the wound had healed. He also had arthritis in his right elbow, both knees and several vertebrae, though not severe enough to be crippling.

science.text: Watson Brake in Louisiana, dated to about 3500 BCE, is considered the oldest earthwork mound complex in North America. It is older than the Egyptian pyramids or Stonehenge. It was built over centuries by hunter-gatherers, who planned and organized large work forces.

The Clovis spear point is found at nearly all locations in North America. Its large, fluted shape allowed it to be hafted onto the end of a spear. The bifacial points were very well made and utilitarian.

The Clovis First theory held that the Clovis culture was the earliest human presence in the Americas, about 13,000 years ago. Evidence of pre-Clovis cultures has since accumulated and pushed back the possible date of the first peopling of the Americas.

Dogs arrived in the Americas about 10,000 years ago alongside Paleo-Indians. The timing of the Koster dogs shows that dogs entered North America from Siberia 4,500 years after humans did. They were then isolated for 9,000 years.

Researchers debate whether the Clovis point tipped a handheld thrusting spear, a throwing spear, or an atlatl. It could well have been used for all three, and also as a knife, as the bifacial point was very well made and utilitarian.

The only empirically based evidence is that Clovis people hunted and killed large game. They also killed small game, but its remains are always found alongside large game at kill sites. Clovis points are large enough to kill, and they turn up at multiple kill sites with megafauna that is now extinct. Studies show even light hunting of large animals can cause extinction, but most data supports climate change as the cause.

The Swan Point Archaeological Site in Alaska has yielded the oldest undisputed evidence of human habitation. Its artifacts have radiocarbon dates of 14,000 years, indicating the site was occupied around 12,000 BCE.

A 2018 study compared North American dog fossils with Siberian dog fossils and modern dogs. The nearest relative was a 9,000 BC fossil from Zhokhov Island in Arctic north-eastern Siberia, which was then connected to the mainland. The study used mDNA to infer that the North American dogs shared a common ancestor.
Around 8000 BC, enough rain fell on the American Southwest to support many large mammal species, including mammoth, mastodon, and a bison species. These animals soon went extinct.

Clovis points were typically made from high-quality silicates such as flint or chert. They are often found hundreds of miles from their source stone, in caches of semi-complete blanks. The makers seem to have buried good material as they traveled, and sometimes forgot where it was.

Cascade points are generally regarded as poor temporal markers because they turn up in early, middle and even late Holocene contexts. It is unclear whether this is due to prolonged use of the point form, later groups recycling discarded artifacts, or both.

Stanford and Bradley theorize that people using atlatl-style hunting on Arctic ice, in groups covering seal breathing holes, could have followed the wrong group of seals back to North America. They would then have adapted this spear-based bifacial technology to the new environment. This would imply that these Paleo-Natives had boat technology.

Foliate projectile points meeting the definition of the Cascade point type were uncovered at a stratified rockshelter in Oregon's Warner Valley. They were associated with a late early Holocene and middle Holocene occupation.

politics.text: Watson Brake in Louisiana, begun about 3500 BCE, is considered the oldest earthwork mound complex in North America. Its discovery in 1997 forced archaeologists to revise the date of the oldest earthwork construction by nearly 2000 years. It is older than the Egyptian pyramids and Stonehenge.

Watson Brake was built by hunter-gatherers, not by a settled maize-farming society with a hierarchical, centralized polity. Archaeologists had expected that pattern at later mound sites. The discovery showed that such peoples could plan and organize large work forces over centuries.

The first mound building is seen as an early marker of political and social complexity among cultures in the eastern part of what is now the United States. Watson Brake, built about 3500 BCE, is the oldest known and dated mound complex in North America.

Watson Brake consists of eleven earthwork mounds, from three to 25 feet in height. Ridges connect them to form an oval nearly 900 feet across. It sits in the floodplain of the Ouachita River, near present-day Monroe in northern Louisiana.

A paper published in 1997 dated Watson Brake and changed how archaeologists saw ancient cultures of the Southeastern United States. They had to revise the date of the oldest earthwork construction by nearly 2000 years.

Since the 1990s, secure dating of Middle Archaic sites in northern Louisiana, Mississippi and Florida has challenged traditional models of development. Hunter-gatherer societies in the Lower Mississippi Valley built monumental mound complexes as early as 3500 BC. Frenchman's Bend and Hedgepeth were early sites, each built by localized societies.

Mound construction at Watson Brake began around 3500 BCE and continued for approximately 500 years, with the mounds enlarged in several stages. There was enough time between building episodes for residents' midden deposits to accumulate on top of the mounds and ridges.

Middle Archaic mound construction seems to have ceased about 2800 BCE. Scholars have not determined why, but changes in river patterns or other environmental factors may have played a part. Watson Brake is one of 11 mound complexes from this period in the Lower Mississippi Valley.
Horr's Island in Southwest Florida included a burial mound dated to 3400 BCE. This makes it the oldest known burial mound in North America, and it was built around the same time as Watson Brake.

Native peoples of the Archaic stage built large earthworks such as Watson Brake, which dates to 3500 BCE. The Mound Builders raised these structures as hunter-gatherer communities were developing complex societies.
politics.source_title: Native Americans in the United States

politics.text: Analysis of 27 radiocarbon dates indicates that Watson Brake was first occupied around 4000 BCE. Teams from the University of Texas at Austin and the University of Washington also dated the site using sand grains and organic acids in the soils.

culture.text: The first people in North America were Paleo-Indian hunter-gatherers. They entered from the North Asian Mammoth steppe across the Beringia land bridge, which formed between northeastern Siberia and western Alaska when sea level dropped during the Last Glacial Maximum.

Indigenous peoples of the Americas have used peyote for over 5,000 years for ceremonial, spiritual and folk medicine purposes. This small, spineless cactus contains psychoactive alkaloids, particularly mescaline. It is native to southern North America, especially northern Mexico and south Texas.
Dogs arrived in the Americas about 10,000 years ago alongside Paleo-Indians. Their descendants today make up a fraction of dog breeds, ranging from the Alaskan Malamute to the Peruvian Hairless Dog.

In 2005, researchers dated two peyote buttons from Shumla Cave No. 5 on the Rio Grande in Texas to between 3780 and 3660 BCE. This suggests native North Americans were likely using peyote at least 5500 years ago.

The most generally accepted theory says Ancient Beringians followed herds of now-extinct Pleistocene megafauna. They traveled along ice-free corridors that stretched between the Laurentide and Cordilleran ice sheets.
The Old Copper complex is cited as an example of early cold working, meaning the hammering of near-pure copper, from around 6,500 BC. This came well before the later copper smelting cultures.

The Shumla Cave No. 5 peyote buttons underwent alkaloid extraction, which yielded approximately 2% of the alkaloids, including mescaline, in both samples. Radiocarbon dating and this alkaloid analysis together showed the cactus was being used in prehistoric North America.
